title: LoRA
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze the model, train small rank-decomposition matrices — the PEFT method that started it all.
details: LoRA freezes pretrained weights W and learns a low-rank update ΔW = BA (B: d×r, A: r×k, r << d), added at inference with zero latency overhead (matrices can be merged). With r=8-64, trainable parameters drop to <1% while matching full fine-tuning on many tasks. Adapters are tiny, swappable, and composable — the foundation of the PEFT ecosystem (Hugging Face PEFT library).
memory_profile: Base in fp16 + tiny adapters; fits 7B on 24GB

demo.title: LoRA reparameterization
demo.program:
import torch
d, r, k = 4096, 8, 4096
W = torch.randn(d, k); A = torch.randn(r, k) * 0.01; B = torch.zeros(d, r)
W_eff = W + (B @ A) * (16 / r)
print(f"trainable {A.numel()+B.numel():,} vs full {W.numel():,} "
      f"({(A.numel()+B.numel())/W.numel():.2%})")

title: QLoRA
summary: LoRA on a 4-bit quantized base model: fine-tune 65B models on a single 48GB GPU.
details: QLoRA combines 4-bit NormalFloat quantization of the frozen base with LoRA adapters, plus paged optimizers and double quantization. The landmark result: fine-tuning a 65B model on one 48GB GPU with quality near full fine-tuning. It democratized large-model fine-tuning overnight; bitsandbytes provides the 4-bit kernels.

demo.title: QLoRA memory math
demo.program:
params_b = 65
print(f"65B: fp16 {params_b*2}GB -> NF4 {params_b*0.5:.0f}GB + adapters/optimizer")

title: LoHa
summary: Hadamard-product low-rank adaptation: more expressive updates per parameter than LoRA.
details: LoHa (from the LyCORIS project) replaces LoRA's single low-rank product with the Hadamard (element-wise) product of two low-rank matrices: ΔW = (B1A1) ⊙ (B2A2). The element-wise product creates higher-rank effective updates from the same parameter budget, often beating LoRA on style/subject learning (its diffusion-model origins). Same drop-in usage as LoRA.

demo.title: LoHa effective rank
demo.program:
import torch
r, d = 8, 256
A1, B1 = torch.randn(r, d), torch.randn(d, r)
A2, B2 = torch.randn(r, d), torch.randn(d, r)
dW = (B1 @ A1) * (B2 @ A2)
print("effective rank:", torch.linalg.matrix_rank(dW).item(), f"(r={r} each)")

title: LoKr
summary: Kronecker-product adaptation: big effective updates from tiny factor matrices.
details: LoKr (LyCORIS) builds ΔW as the Kronecker product of two small matrices: ΔW = B ⊗ A. The Kronecker structure yields very high-rank updates from few parameters — parameter efficiency beyond LoRA/LoHa. Best for cases needing large-capacity adaptation on a tight budget; tuning the factor shapes matters.
params_trained: Fewer than LoRA for same effective rank

demo.title: Kronecker expansion
demo.program:
import torch
A, B = torch.randn(4, 8), torch.randn(8, 4)
dW = torch.kron(B, A)
print(f"factors {A.numel()+B.numel()} params -> {dW.numel()} update params")

title: AdaLoRA
summary: Adaptive budget allocation: give more rank to important layers, less to unimportant ones.
details: AdaLoRA parameterizes updates via SVD-like decomposition and adaptively prunes singular values by importance scores during training — important layers keep high rank, unimportant ones shrink. Same total budget as LoRA, better used. Particularly effective when you do not know which layers matter for your task.
params_trained: Same budget as LoRA, adaptively allocated

demo.title: Rank allocation by importance

title: DoRA
summary: Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation: separate magnitude and direction for fuller fine-tuning.
details: DoRA decomposes each weight into magnitude and direction components, applying LoRA-style updates to the direction while learning magnitudes separately. This mimics full fine-tuning's learning pattern more closely than LoRA and consistently outperforms it, at modest extra cost (magnitude vector). A strong default upgrade over vanilla LoRA.
when_to_use: When LoRA quality is not quite enough

demo.title: DoRA decomposition
demo.program:
import torch
W = torch.randn(256, 256)
mag = W.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
direction = W / mag
print("magnitude shape:", tuple(mag.shape), "| direction unit-norm:",
      bool(torch.allclose(direction.norm(dim=1), torch.ones(256), atol=1e-5)))

title: Houlsby Adapters
summary: The original adapters: small bottleneck MLPs inserted between transformer layers.
details: Houlsby adapters (2019) insert bottleneck feed-forward modules (down-project, nonlinearity, up-project) after attention and FFN sublayers, training only the adapters. They launched the PEFT field and remain competitive; unlike LoRA they add inference latency (extra layers), but their modularity suits multi-task setups where adapters swap per task.

demo.title: Adapter bottleneck
demo.program:
import torch, torch.nn as nn
ad = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(768, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 768))
x = torch.randn(2, 10, 768)
print("adapter params:", sum(p.numel() for p in ad.parameters()))

title: Prefix Tuning
summary: Learn continuous prefix vectors prepended to keys/values — the model stays frozen.
details: Prefix tuning prepends learned continuous vectors to the keys and values at every layer (a reparameterized MLP generates them for stability). Only ~0.1% parameters train. It matches full fine-tuning on generation tasks with tiny storage per task — but optimization is trickier than LoRA, and it adds prefix length to every forward pass.

demo.title: Prefix shapes
demo.program:
layers, prefix_len, hidden = 12, 20, 768
print(f"prefix params: {2*layers*prefix_len*hidden:,} "
      f"({2*layers*prefix_len*hidden/110e6:.2%} of 110M)")

title: Prompt Tuning
summary: The simplest PEFT: learn soft prompt embeddings prepended to the input.
details: Prompt tuning learns a handful of continuous 'soft prompt' embeddings prepended to input embeddings; everything else frozen. At <0.01% parameters it works well on large models (11B+) but underperforms on smaller ones. Lester et al. showed scale compensates for the tiny capacity — the minimalist's fine-tune.

demo.title: Soft prompt params
demo.program:
tokens, hidden = 20, 4096
print(f"soft prompt: {tokens*hidden:,} params")

title: P-Tuning v2
summary: Deep prompt tuning: prompts at every layer, closing the gap to fine-tuning.
details: P-Tuning v2 adds trainable prompts to every transformer layer (not just input), matching full fine-tuning across scales (300M-10B) on NLU tasks with 0.1-3% parameters. It fixed v1's optimization issues and remains the strongest prompt-based method for smaller models.

demo.title: Deep prompt count
demo.program:
layers, plen, h = 24, 100, 1024
print(f"deep prompts: {layers*plen*h/1e6:.1f}M params")

title: IA3
summary: Three learned vectors per layer rescale attention and FFN — the most parameter-frugal adapter.
details: (IA)^3 learns three vectors per transformer block that rescale keys, values, and FFN activations by element-wise multiplication. At ~0.01% parameters it matches or beats adapters on many tasks, and the rescaling fuses into weights for zero inference overhead. The efficiency champion for multi-task serving.

demo.title: IA3 rescaling
demo.program:
import torch
x = torch.randn(4, 8)
scale = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.ones(8))
print("rescaled:", (x * scale).shape, "| params:", scale.numel())

title: BitFit
summary: Train only the bias terms — 0.1% of parameters, surprisingly competitive.
details: BitFit freezes everything except bias vectors (~0.1% of parameters) and still matches full fine-tuning on several GLUE tasks. The finding: much task adaptation lives in the biases. It is the simplest possible PEFT baseline and a useful sanity check — if BitFit works, you do not need heavier methods.

demo.title: Bias-only params
demo.program:
import torch.nn as nn
m = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(512, 8, batch_first=True)
total = sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())
bias = sum(p.numel() for n, p in m.named_parameters() if "bias" in n)
print(f"bias {bias:,} / total {total:,} = {bias/total:.2%}")

title: LLaMA-Adapter
summary: Lightweight adaptation for LLaMA with zero-init attention gates.
details: LLaMA-Adapter inserts learnable adaptation prompts into the top transformer layers with zero-initialized gating — starting as identity, so training is stable from step one. Version 2 extends to more parameters unlocked progressively. Designed for instruction-following on LLaMA with ~1M trainable parameters.

demo.title: Zero-init gate
demo.program:
import torch
gate = torch.zeros(1)  # starts as identity
print("gate:", float(gate), "-> learns to open during training")

title: ReLoRA
summary: High-rank training via periodic LoRA merges — full-rank updates at LoRA cost.
details: ReLoRA trains LoRA adapters, periodically merges them into the base weights, and re-initializes fresh adapters — accumulating high-rank updates over time at LoRA's memory cost. With optimizer-state resets tuned carefully, it approaches full-rank training efficiency. For pretraining-from-scratch on a budget.

demo.title: Merge-and-restart cycle
demo.program:
import torch
W = torch.zeros(64, 64); A, B = torch.randn(8, 64)*0.01, torch.zeros(64, 8)
W = W + B @ A  # merge
A, B = torch.randn(8, 64)*0.01, torch.zeros(64, 8)  # restart
print("merged once; new adapters ready")

title: GaLore
summary: Gradient Low-Rank Projection: full-parameter training with LoRA-sized optimizer states.
details: GaLore projects gradients into a low-rank subspace for the optimizer update, then projects back — training ALL parameters while optimizer states stay small. Unlike LoRA it is full-parameter learning (better for pretraining), with memory near LoRA levels. The subspace updates periodically via SVD of gradients.

demo.title: Gradient projection sketch
demo.program:
import torch
G = torch.randn(256, 256)
U, _, _ = torch.svd_lowrank(G, q=16)
G_low = U @ (U.T @ G)
print(f"projected {G.numel():,} grad -> rank-16 subspace")

title: LISA
summary: Layerwise Importance Sampling: train only the most important layers each step.
details: LISA samples layers by importance (embedding/norm layers always, others sampled) and updates only those — cutting memory to LoRA levels while updating real weights. It matches or beats LoRA on instruction tuning with a delightfully simple mechanism: not all layers need updating all the time.
when_to_use: Simple full-ish tuning on tight memory

demo.title: Layer sampling
demo.program:
import random
random.seed(0)
layers = list(range(32))
active = [0, 31] + random.sample(layers[1:31], 4)
print("updating layers:", sorted(active))

title: rsLoRA
summary: Rank-Stabilized LoRA: fix LoRA's scaling so higher ranks actually help.
details: Standard LoRA's scaling (alpha/r) collapses gradients at high rank, so increasing r stops helping. rsLoRA changes scaling to alpha/sqrt(r), making higher ranks compute-optimal — rank 64+ keeps improving. A one-line change that rescues high-rank LoRA runs.

demo.title: Scaling comparison

title: PiSSA
summary: Principal Singular values and Singular vectors Adaptation: init adapters from the top SVD.
details: PiSSA initializes LoRA's A/B from the principal singular components of W (instead of random/zero), so adapters start from the most important directions. Faster convergence and better final quality than vanilla LoRA at identical cost — a strictly better initialization.

demo.title: SVD init sketch
demo.program:
import torch
W = torch.randn(256, 256)
U, S, Vh = torch.linalg.svd(W, full_matrices=False)
r = 8
A, B = (U[:, :r]*S[:r]).T, Vh[:r, :].T
print("adapter init from top-8 singular directions")

title: Multi-LoRA Serving
summary: Serve many LoRAs on one base model — the deployment pattern for personalized fine-tunes.
details: Multi-LoRA serving (vLLM, SGLang, LoRAX) batches requests across hundreds of adapters on a single base model, applying each adapter's update only to its tokens. One GPU fleet serves thousands of personalized models. The PEFT method that made 'a fine-tune per customer' economical.

demo.title: Adapter batching
demo.program:
reqs = [("a", "lora_1"), ("b", "lora_2"), ("c", "lora_1")]
from itertools import groupby
for ad, g in groupby(sorted(reqs, key=lambda x: x[1]), key=lambda x: x[1]):
    print(ad, "serves", [r[0] for r in g])

title: Merging LoRA Weights
summary: Combine multiple LoRAs by weighted sum — multi-task adapters without retraining.
details: LoRA adapters for different tasks can be merged by weighted averaging (or TIES/SLERP-style methods) into one adapter with combined capabilities. It is the cheapest multi-tasking: train specialists, merge generalists. Weighting by task importance or learned coefficients tunes the blend.

demo.title: Weighted LoRA merge
demo.program:
import torch
lora_a = torch.randn(8, 64); lora_b = torch.randn(8, 64)
merged = 0.6*lora_a + 0.4*lora_b
print("merged adapter:", tuple(merged.shape))

title: LoRA+ (Differential LR)
summary: Train B faster than A: one-line LR tweak that speeds and improves LoRA.
details: LoRA+ sets the learning rate for B (the zero-initialized matrix) higher than for A — fixing LoRA's inefficient feature learning. The result: faster convergence and better final performance at zero extra cost. If you run LoRA, set lora_b_lr > lora_a_lr.

demo.title: Differential LRs
demo.program:
opt_groups = [{"params": "A", "lr": 1e-4}, {"params": "B", "lr": 1e-3}]
print("B learns 10x faster:", opt_groups)

title: VeRA
summary: Vector-based Random Matrix Adaptation: freeze random matrices, train only scaling vectors.
details: VeRA freezes shared random matrices across layers and trains only tiny scaling vectors per layer — 10x fewer parameters than LoRA with competitive quality. All layers share the random pair; per-layer vectors adapt them. The extreme-efficiency option when storage is everything.

demo.title: VeRA sharing
demo.program:
layers, d, r = 32, 4096, 256
shared = 2*d*r
per_layer = 2*d
print(f"shared {shared/1e6:.0f}M + {layers} x {per_layer/1e3:.0f}K vectors")

title: BOFT
summary: Butterfly Orthogonal Fine-Tuning: orthogonal updates via butterfly factorization.
details: BOFT parameterizes updates as products of butterfly-structured orthogonal matrices — preserving weight norms (stable training) with O(d log d) parameters. Orthogonality prevents the rank-collapse issues of plain LoRA and suits tasks needing stable, well-conditioned adaptation.

demo.title: Butterfly params
demo.program:
import math
d = 4096
print(f"butterfly params ~ {d*math.log2(d):,.0f} vs LoRA r=8: {2*d*8:,}")

title: LongLoRA
summary: Extend context during fine-tuning: LoRA plus shifted sparse attention for long contexts.
details: LongLoRA fine-tunes models to long contexts (100K) cheaply: LoRA adapters plus shifted short attention (S2-Attn) during training, with full attention restored at inference. It made long-context extension a fine-tuning job instead of a pretraining job.

demo.title: Shifted sparse attention groups
demo.program:
seq, group = 32768, 8192
print(f"{seq} tokens -> {seq//group} groups; shift by half for cross-talk")

title: MoRA
summary: High-rank updating via square matrices: more capacity than LoRA at the same budget.
details: MoRA replaces LoRA's low-rank factors with square matrices plus compression/decompression operators, achieving high-rank updates with the same parameter count as LoRA. It closes the gap to full fine-tuning on memory-intensive tasks (e.g., math/code) where LoRA's rank bottleneck shows.
params_trained: Same count as LoRA, higher rank

demo.title: Square vs low-rank
demo.program:
r, d = 8, 4096
lora_rank = r
mora_rank = 256  # same param budget, higher effective rank
print(f"LoRA rank {lora_rank} vs MoRA effective rank {mora_rank}")
